clinicalPearls: A localised neuropathic itch, often with burning or stinging, affecting the dorsolateral forearms over the brachioradialis region, which may extend to the upper arms and shoulders
It is typically bilateral, though often asymmetrical, and characteristically worse in summer and in fair-skinned people with substantial sun exposure
The 'ice-pack sign' is highly characteristic: patients gain relief from applying something cold rather than from scratching, which distinguishes it from most other pruritic conditions
There is a recognised association with cervical spine disease such as degenerative change or nerve-root compression, and the affected dermatomes often correspond to lower cervical levels
The interplay of chronic ultraviolet exposure and underlying cervical nerve pathology is thought to sensitise cutaneous nerves and produce the itch
The skin may look normal or show only secondary excoriation and lichenification from rubbing
Management combines photoprotection with neuropathic-itch measures and, where relevant, assessment and treatment of cervical spine pathology
reference.pathophysiology: Brachioradial pruritus is understood as a neuropathic itch arising from dysfunction of cutaneous sensory nerves, in which chronic ultraviolet-induced damage to nerve endings acts together with proximal cervical nerve-root irritation from degenerative spine disease to lower the threshold for itch signalling. The characteristic relief from cold and the frequent correspondence of symptoms to cervical dermatomes support a neurogenic rather than a primary inflammatory mechanism. The summer predominance reflects the contribution of accumulated sun exposure to peripheral nerve sensitisation.
additionalDifferentials: Notalgia paraesthetica and other neuropathic localised pruritus
Cervical radiculopathy or spinal cord pathology presenting with itch
Atopic or contact dermatitis of the forearms
additionalInvestigations: History elicting the ice-pack sign, summer predominance and forearm localisation
Neurological examination and assessment for cervical spine disease
Imaging of the cervical spine (radiography or magnetic resonance imaging) where radiculopathy is suspected
Phototesting only if a primary photodermatosis is being considered
Skin biopsy in atypical cases, which is usually non-specific
Review of the pattern to exclude a systemic cause of generalised pruritus
redFlags: Neurological deficit, limb weakness or sensory loss suggesting significant cervical cord or nerve-root compression
Rapidly progressive or unilateral symptoms warranting spinal imaging
Features of an inflammatory dermatosis or systemic pruritus that do not fit a neuropathic pattern
Intractable itch with severe secondary skin damage
reference.prognosis: Brachioradial pruritus tends to be chronic and relapsing with a seasonal, sun-related pattern, but symptoms are often controllable with photoprotection, cold application and neuropathic-itch therapy; addressing any underlying cervical spine pathology can improve outcomes, though complete resolution is variable.
pitfalls: Treating it as an inflammatory dermatitis with topical steroids alone, which are generally ineffective for neuropathic itch
Overlooking the ice-pack sign, which is a valuable diagnostic clue
Failing to consider and investigate underlying cervical spine disease
Not advising photoprotection despite the clear relationship with sun exposure
references: British Association of Dermatologists resources on pruritus
management: Rigorous photoprotection and sun avoidance to reduce the ultraviolet-driven cutaneous nerve sensitisation
Cold application, exploiting the characteristic ice-pack sign, for symptomatic relief
Topical neuropathic agents such as capsaicin or topical anaesthetics for localised itch
Systemic neuropathic-itch therapy such as gabapentin or pregabalin for refractory symptoms
Assessment and treatment of underlying cervical spine disease, including physiotherapy
Discouraging the scratch-itch cycle to limit excoriation and lichenification
Referral to neurology or spinal services when cervical radiculopathy is contributory
